notes.b: Novel (alternative) protein foods replace meat, fish or eggs in the diet. They come from two kinds of source: plants, and micro-organisms (living things too small to see without a microscope, grown in large quantities).
points: Soya beans are the main plant source. They are made into tofu, tempeh, textured vegetable protein (TVP), miso, soya milk, soya yoghurt and soya cheese, and also soya flour, soya sauce and soya oil.

Other plant products include seitan, which is made from wheat gluten (the protein part of wheat), and pulses such as lentils, chickpeas and beans. Nuts and seeds, quinoa, edamame and hummus also supply plant protein.
The micro-organism sources are fungi, bacteria, yeast and algae.

Mycoprotein is a protein food made from a fungus grown by fermentation (growing it in a controlled tank), so it is a micro-organism product and not a plant. It is sold as Quorn in mince, pieces, burgers and sausages. Quorn is a brand name; the general term is mycoprotein.
Nutritional yeast is a yeast product used as a flavouring in vegan cooking and, when fortified, as a source of B vitamins. It is also used as a source of protein in vegan cooking.
notes.tip: A table question asks you to match source to product: plant, soya beans, with TVP, tofu, tempeh, miso and soya milk; micro-organisms (fungi, bacteria, yeast, algae), with mycoprotein or Quorn. Name the micro-organism source as a fungus, not a plant.

notes.h: Soya products and how they are made
notes.b: Soya beans are turned into several quite different foods, and the way each is made explains its texture and taste. Some are curdled or ground, others are fermented (changed by moulds, bacteria or yeast).
points: Tofu: soya milk is curdled and the curds are pressed into blocks. It is bland, so it takes on flavour from marinades or smoking.
Soya milk: soaked soya beans are ground with their soaking water and the mixture is strained, which removes the solid pulp.
Tempeh: cooked soya beans are fermented by a mould, giving a firm, chewy texture. Because the whole beans are used, it is not the same as tofu, which is made from curd.
Miso: soya beans are mixed with rice (or another grain), salt and water and fermented into a paste.
Soya yoghurt: soya milk is fermented in the same way as dairy yoghurt.
notes.tip: Keep the three apart in an answer: tofu is curd, tempeh is fermented whole beans, miso is a fermented paste. TVP is a different product again, made from defatted soya flour and not from curd.

notes.b: TVP is a meat substitute made from soya flour that has had its oil removed. The aim of the process is to turn a protein-rich flour into a fibrous, chewy product, so learn the stages in order.
points: 1. Soya beans are cleaned and de-hulled (their outer skins are removed), and their oil is extracted.
2. The de-oiled beans are ground into flour.
3. Carbohydrate is removed, leaving a protein-rich flour.
4. Vegetable oil, flavourings, seasonings and nutritional additives such as vitamin B12, iron and methionine (an amino acid) are added, which improves the taste and nutritional value.
5. The mixture is heated and extruded (forced through a machine under pressure), which forms a textured, fibrous product.
6. The product is cut, cubed or chopped into pieces such as mince or chunks.
7. The pieces are dried, packed and labelled.
notes.tip: Manufacture questions ask you to name the product and outline its stages. Learn the TVP stages in order and give at least five. Do not confuse TVP with tofu.

notes.b: Mycoprotein is grown rather than farmed or pressed. A fungus is multiplied in tanks and then shaped into a meat-like food in a series of stages.
points: 1. A fungus is fermented (grown) in carefully controlled conditions so that it grows in large quantities.
2. The fungal cells are harvested, filtered and drained.
3. A binder holds the fungal sheets together, and flavour and colour are added. The traditional product uses egg albumen as the binder.
4. The mass is textured to resemble meat.
5. It is sliced, cubed or shredded, steamed to set the binder, then packed and labelled.
notes.tip: Name the micro-organism source as a fungus and say it is grown by fermentation. Do not name a species. Not all mycoprotein is vegan, because the traditional binder is egg albumen, so say check the label.

notes.h: Nutritional significance and contribution to the diet
notes.b: Soya and mycoprotein products can supply protein in place of meat, but their nutritional value depends on the product.
points: Soya protein is high biological value (it supplies all the essential amino acids in good proportions). Soya products also supply polyunsaturated fat, fibre and B group vitamins.
Calcium and iron are present in many soya products, especially tofu set with calcium salts.
Mycoprotein is relatively high in protein and fibre and low in saturated fat. Plant alternatives contain no cholesterol.

Advantages of alternatives: they supply high biological value protein, are low in saturated fat and contain fibre. They suit vegetarians and vegans, are relatively inexpensive and versatile, need little preparation and reduce reliance on meat.
Plant foods contain no vitamin B12, so vegans need it from fortified foods or supplements.
Processed alternatives may be high in salt, sugar and additives, so their labels should be checked. Soya is a labelled allergen, and Quorn contains egg in some products.
In the Food Pyramid of the Department of Health healthy eating guidelines, these foods sit on the shelf of meat, poultry, fish, eggs, beans and nuts, which supplies protein and iron.
These foods can replace meat in meals, be used as meat extenders (mixed with meat to make it go further) and be eaten in vegetarian and vegan diets.
notes.tip: If asked for two advantages of a protein alternative for a vegan diet, give nutrients with a reason, such as high biological value protein, polyunsaturated fat, fibre, B vitamins, calcium or iron, or practical points such as not very expensive, versatile and little preparation. Plant-based does not automatically mean healthy, because ultra-processed versions can be high in salt and additives.

notes.b: Choosing and handling these foods well depends mostly on reading the label and following the pack, because each product keeps and prepares differently.
points: When selecting, read the label for ingredients, allergens, nutrition information and use-by date. Compare salt, sugar and fat in processed alternatives.

Labels must show ingredients, allergens and a nutrition declaration, under Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, given effect in Ireland by the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014.
Dried TVP and dried pulses keep in airtight containers in a cool, dry place, which keeps moisture and pests out.
TVP must be rehydrated in hot stock or water before use, and it takes on the flavour of the liquid.
Tofu is sold chilled or in sealed packs. Once opened it should be kept under fresh water, with a lid or cover, in the refrigerator and used within the number of days on the label.
Tofu is drained and pressed before frying, so that it browns well and holds its shape.
Pulses are soaked and boiled before use, or bought tinned and ready to use.
Mycoprotein products are sold chilled or frozen and should be cooked thoroughly as the pack directs. Follow the pack instructions for all of these products.
notes.tip: Plant-based alternatives are not automatically healthy, because ultra-processed versions can be high in salt and additives, so check the label. Storage differs by food: dried TVP and pulses airtight, cool and dry; tofu and mycoprotein chilled or frozen.

notes.b: Most alternatives have little taste or texture of their own, so processing and cooking are what make them appealing and meat-like.
points: Extrusion gives textured vegetable protein its fibrous, chewy texture, which resembles meat.
Marinating or smoking gives tofu flavour, as it is bland on its own. It can then be marinated and stir-fried or baked.
Fermentation by moulds or bacteria gives tempeh, miso and soya yoghurt their texture and flavour.
Mycoprotein is shaped and then steamed to set its binder, so that the pieces hold together during cooking. It must be cooked thoroughly as the pack directs.
TVP is used in dishes such as bolognese, chilli and shepherd's pie. TVP, tofu and mycoprotein take on the flavour of what they are cooked in, so seasoning and sauces matter.
notes.tip: Remember that seitan is made from wheat gluten, so it is unsuitable for a coeliac diet (a diet that must avoid gluten), and soya is a labelled allergen.

notes.h: Evaluating protein bars and high-protein products
notes.b: Protein bars and high-protein products should be judged from the label data rather than from the words high protein on the packet. A high-protein claim does not make a product healthy.
points: Compare per portion the protein, energy, sugar, saturated fat, salt and fibre, not the protein claim alone.
Bars often contain added sugar, a chocolate coating, saturated fat and salt, so check these as well as the protein.

Protein bars may be made with milk (whey) protein or soya protein, which supply high biological value protein. Bars are portable, which makes them most useful where portability is needed, such as for sport.
A high-protein fruit yoghurt supplies high biological value milk protein, calcium, phosphorus and B group vitamins.
Sweetened fruit preparations raise the free sugar content of a yoghurt. Full-fat versions contain more saturated fat, and low-fat versions may contain more added sugar.
Plain yoghurt with fresh fruit is generally the less processed choice.

Under EU nutrition claims rules (Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006), a food can claim to be a source of protein if at least 12% of its energy comes from protein. It can claim to be high protein if at least 20% of its energy comes from protein.
When reading a data table, pick the product with the most protein and fibre and the least energy, sugar and salt for the person stated, for example a young person who plays sport.
notes.tip: Evaluation questions give label data for bars or yoghurts. Compare protein per serving, energy, sugar, fat, fibre and salt, mention high biological value protein, then recommend one product with reasons. Compare per portion, not just the protein claim.

keyTerms.definition: A protein food made from a plant or micro-organism source to replace meat, fish or eggs in the diet.
A dried, extruded soya product that is rehydrated and used as a meat substitute in mince-type dishes.
A protein food made from a fungus grown by controlled fermentation and textured to resemble meat.
A soya curd made by curdling soya milk and pressing the curds into blocks.
A firm, chewy food made from cooked soya beans fermented by a mould.
A fermented paste made from soya beans, rice, salt and water.
A process in which a heated mixture is forced through a shaped opening, giving it a fibrous texture.
An ingredient that holds the pieces of a textured protein product together during shaping and setting.
Soaking a dried food in liquid so that it regains its moisture before cooking.

questions.prompt: Name two protein alternatives suitable for a vegan diet, and state two nutritional advantages of including them.
questions.model: Two alternatives such as tofu, tempeh, textured vegetable protein, mycoprotein, seitan, soya milk or lentils. Advantages: high biological value protein; polyunsaturated fat; fibre; B group vitamins; calcium and iron (in many soya products); inexpensive and versatile, and quick to prepare.

questions.prompt: Select one novel protein food you have studied, name it, and set out its stages of manufacture.
questions.model: Name the product, for example textured vegetable protein or mycoprotein. For textured vegetable protein: soya beans are cleaned, de-hulled and their oil extracted; the beans are ground to flour; carbohydrate is removed; vegetable oil, flavourings, seasonings and nutritional additives such as vitamin B12, iron and methionine are added; the mixture is heated and extruded; it is cut or cubed into mince-like pieces; it is dried, packed and labelled. For mycoprotein: a fungus is fermented under controlled conditions; the cells are harvested, filtered and drained; a binder is added; flavour and colour are added; the mass is textured, sliced, cubed or shredded and steamed to set the binder; it is packed and labelled.
